Full paper title: Recycling WEEE: extraction and concentration of silver from waste crystalline silicon photovoltaic modules
Authors: Pablo Dias; Selene Javimczik; Mariana Benevit; Hugo Veit; Andréa Moura Bernardes
Research question: Can silver be concentrated from waste c-Si modules, and does a 500 C pyrolysis pretreatment improve the route?
Feed material: Waste crystalline-silicon modules; article identifies first-generation module material
Feed preparation: Aluminium frame removed; module milled and sieved; paper describes selecting particles below 0.5 mm for the chemical route
Module or cell technology: Crystalline silicon; specific cell design and module population are study-specific
Initial silver concentration: 630 g/t reported average in the paper conclusions; abstract rounds this to 600 g/t
Concentration basis: Paper describes an average amount in modules; exact mass denominator relative to frame removal is not unambiguously stated in the accessible metadata
Separation method: Mechanical milling and sieving followed by hydrometallurgical silver concentration; compared with a 500 C pyrolysis pretreatment
Experimental conditions: Abstract reports 64% nitric-acid solution and sodium chloride of 99% stated purity; the latter is not a 99% solution concentration
Silver recovery, if measured: 94% for the route without pyrolysis; 92% with pyrolysis, reported as silver concentration yield
Other reported recovery metrics: The paper concludes pyrolysis did not improve silver extraction; non-pyrolysis route used less energy qualitatively
Analytical method: Paper metadata reports XRF characterization and Ag quantification; accessible record mentions five XRF measurements for one table
Number of replicates, if reported: Five XRF measurements are shown for one characterization table; process replicate count not established from accessible abstract/metadata
Energy or reagent consumption: Pyrolysis at 500 C in the comparator; no numerical energy use recovered; acid and salt used in both routes
Main findings: Study-specific module silver benchmark and reported 94% versus 92% silver yield; pyrolysis did not help the silver result
Study limitations: Older module feed; source abstract and repository record do not establish a common denominator with the 300 ppm review scenario; chemical route is outside the current dry Stage 3
Relevance to AGASTYA: Useful historical feed benchmark and competing mechanical-plus-chemical route; not a forecast for AGASTYA
Data extraction status: Abstract plus university repository metadata and indexed article snippets; full article tables not independently re-extracted
Verification status: Metadata, DOI, abstract and reported conclusions cross-checked on publisher/university pages
Numerical value source location: Publisher abstract and indexed Conclusions snippet; university repository abstract lines 15-17
Value provenance: 630 g/t and 94/92% are author-reported experimental values; 600 g/t is the rounded abstract phrase
Interpretation and data handling notes: Retain 630 g/t as a separate study benchmark. Do not merge it with module composition reviews or convert it into an AGASTYA assay.

Full paper title: Rethinking silver recovery pathways in end-of-life photovoltaic recycling using froth flotation
Authors: Hamidreza Saffarian; Kevin P. Galvin; Mahshid Firouzi
Peer-review status: Publisher classifies as research article; open-access article
Research question: Can froth flotation selectively pre-concentrate metallic silver from delaminated end-of-life solar cells?
Feed material: Real delaminated solar-cell feed supplied by industry partners; not whole modules
Feed preparation: 3.5 kg crushed-cell feed, homogenized, d100 2 mm, wet ground to d80 103 micrometres; assay-by-size and riffle splitting
Module or cell technology: End-of-life crystalline-silicon cells; exact mix of cell generations not resolved in accessible text
Initial feed mass, if reported: 3.5 kg prepared feed; 110 g per 1 L flotation test in the reported triplicate tap-water table
Initial silver concentration: The tap-water table reports a mean feed assay of about 0.75 wt% Ag for prepared cell feed
Concentration basis: Prepared and ground cell feed, not full-module mass; ICP-MS values are described as total-recoverable Ag
Separation method: Rougher froth flotation; rougher-cleaner flotation evaluated as a concentration option
Experimental conditions: 1 L mechanical cell, about 7 wt% solids, matched tip speed about 5.3 m/s, natural pH; reported reagent dosage 150 g/t dry feed; tap-water triplicate and ultrapure-water cases
Silver recovery, if measured: Tap-water rougher 97.55 +/- 0.03%; ultrapure-water 1 L rougher 91.30 +/- 0.61%; rougher-cleaner 86.5 +/- 2.8%
Silver concentration in product: Tap-water rougher upgrade 32.2 +/- 2.3 times; rougher-cleaner concentrate 46.7 +/- 1.5 wt% Ag
Product mass, if reported: Tap-water table reports mean concentrate about 3.11 g from a 110 g feed test; rougher-cleaner concentrate mass not captured here
Other reported recovery metrics: About 2.8 wt% of feed reports to 3-minute rougher concentrate in tap-water case; cleaner case about 1.4 wt% feed to leach is a paper mass-balance illustration
Analytical method: ICP-MS on digested feed, concentrates and tailings; independent ALS fire assay used as benchmark; TIMA/SEM-EDS for mineralogical and liberation analysis
Number of replicates, if reported: Three tap-water tests at the stated rougher condition; other condition replicate counts not captured here
Measurement uncertainty: Tap-water recovery +/-0.03 percentage point and upgrade +/-2.3 times, as reported; table reports SD/SE as well
Energy or reagent consumption: Reagent dosage reported at 150 g/t dry feed; water use and energy were not reported as lifecycle totals
Main findings: Direct measured Ag recovery and upgrade for prepared PV-cell feed; cleaning traded some recovery for a roughly 47 wt% Ag product
Study limitations: Bench-scale single research campaign, specific delaminated cell feed, reagent-dependent, and not a direct comparison with electrostatic tests on different feed
Relevance to AGASTYA: Strongest retrieved direct evidence for silver-specific beneficiation and a comparator for any Stage 3 redesign
Data extraction status: Publisher abstract plus indexed accessible full-text methods, results and tables; raw dataset was not retrieved
Verification status: DOI, publication metadata, methods, reported conditions and metrics checked on publisher page
Numerical value source location: Publisher abstract; Sections 2.2, 2.5, 3.1 and 3.5; Table 1 for triplicate tap-water assays
Value provenance: Silver assays and recoveries are author-reported measurements/calculations; simple feed-normalized conversions are project-derived only when explicitly labeled
Interpretation and data handling notes: Do not apply these recoveries to whole-module feed or multiply them by unrelated Stage 1/2 yields. Grade, recovery and concentrate mass are separate quantities.

Full paper title: Study of electrostatic separation to concentrate silver, aluminum, and silicon from solar panel scraps
Authors: Rodrigo A. de Souza; Hugo M. Veit
Peer-review status: Journal page identifies original research and provides review-status fields
Research question: Can electrostatic separation concentrate metals of interest from mechanically processed PV scraps?
Feed material: Mechanically processed waste polycrystalline silicon PV panel scrap
Feed preparation: Comminuted and granulometrically classified before electrostatic separation
Module or cell technology: Polycrystalline silicon; paper uses Si-C terminology
Concentration basis: XRF comparisons of elemental proportions in sample fractions; the accessible abstract does not specify whole-module or mass-weighted assay denominator
Separation method: Electrostatic roll separator, with evaluation of applied voltage, roll speed, electrode distance and angle
Experimental conditions: Best conditions reported in the abstract: 38 kV potential difference and 75 rpm; 49.22% of comminuted mass was in the smallest size fraction below 0.5 mm
Silver concentration in product: Qualitative abstract finding: Ag, Al and Si could be concentrated; quantitative product grade not available in abstract
Product mass, if reported: No mass-weighted electrostatic product split available in the abstract; 49.22% refers to pre-separator smallest size fraction
Other reported recovery metrics: XRF elemental proportions were compared; the paper abstract does not provide mass recovery or silver recovery
Energy or reagent consumption: No energy, water or reagent consumption reported in accessible abstract
Main findings: Direct electrostatic test reported co-concentration of silver, aluminum and silicon; not evidence of silver-only separation or a calculated Ag recovery
Study limitations: Full article data and product mass balance were not accessible in the extraction reviewed; particle charge, Ag recovery and product grade remain unavailable
Relevance to AGASTYA: Corrects the prior evidence gap: Stage 3 has direct but incomplete PV-scrap Ag co-concentration evidence
Data extraction status: Abstract-level extraction only; SciOpen page states that full article content is not available on that page
Verification status: Metadata, DOI, authors, publication date, feed description, abstract conditions and results cross-checked on SciOpen and publisher pages
Numerical value source location: Publisher/SciOpen Abstract, lines describing 49.22%, below 0.5 mm, 38 kV and 75 rpm
Value provenance: 49.22%, voltage and speed are author-reported experimental values; no project-derived silver recovery
Interpretation and data handling notes: Treat as evidence of Ag-containing fraction co-concentration, not as a selective Ag recovery percentage.

Full paper title: Recycling Si in waste crystalline silicon photovoltaic panels after mechanical crushing by electrostatic separation
Authors: Jiayan Li; Shuang Yan; Yaoyao Li; Zhiqiang Wang; Yi Tan; Jin Li; Mingxu Xia; Pengting Li
Research question: Can electrostatic separation recover silicon from mechanically crushed c-Si PV waste?
Feed material: Crushed c-Si PV panel waste separated into blocks and mixed powder
Feed preparation: Mechanical crushing, acid washing/XRF characterization, then mixed-powder size classification
Module or cell technology: Crystalline silicon; exact panel generation not captured in abstract
Concentration basis: The study target and reported metrics are silicon, not silver
Experimental conditions: Best Si condition: 0.30-0.45 mm feed, 15 kV and 30 rpm
Silicon recovery, if measured: 48.9% Si recovery; 91.0% Si proportion in recovered product
Other reported recovery metrics: 82.8 wt% of Si in crushed c-Si PV waste was distributed in mixed powder after pretreatment
Energy or reagent consumption: No lifecycle energy or reagent totals reported in abstract
Main findings: Demonstrates Si recovery under a specific size and separator condition; it does not establish Ag recovery
Study limitations: Target metric is silicon; no silver partition or silver mass balance in accessible abstract
Relevance to AGASTYA: Useful counterexample to prevent using Si recovery as an Ag proxy
Verification status: Publisher metadata, DOI and abstract checked
Interpretation and data handling notes: Do not use the 48.9% Si recovery as any silver recovery input.

Full paper title: A facile crush-and-sieve treatment for recycling end-of-life photovoltaics
Authors: Ying Sim; Yeow Boon Tay; Huu Khue Pham; Nripan Mathews
Research question: Can crushing and sieving separate polymer-rich and silver-enriched fractions without thermal burning?
Feed material: Two waste PV module categories identified in the paper as EVAc and MP
Feed preparation: Cutting, mechanical crushing and screening into four size fractions; the accessible abstract does not give feed mass or all screen boundaries
Module or cell technology: Two study-specific waste categories; exact technology labels should be checked against full paper before mapping to mono/poly classes
Concentration basis: Share of total Ag in each study feed category reporting to the smallest size fraction F4
Experimental conditions: Silver was enriched in the smallest particle fraction F4; exact F4 boundaries are not taken from abstract
Silver recovery, if measured: Up to 70% of total Ag in EVAc and 80% in MP feed category reported in F4
Silver concentration in product: Described as silver-enriched fraction; quantitative product Ag grade unavailable in abstract
Other reported recovery metrics: More than 90% of total polymer reported in larger fractions F1 and F2
Analytical method: Metal-content analysis; exact analytical method not captured in accessible abstract
Energy or reagent consumption: No numerical energy use in abstract; route avoids the study's comparator thermal burning step
Main findings: Mechanical size classification can partition substantial study-feed Ag into a small-particle class, with category-specific results
Study limitations: Fraction partition is not product grade or pure Ag; study feeds and size bins may differ from AGASTYA; abstract lacks full feed/product mass details
Relevance to AGASTYA: Strong direct comparator for Stage 2 liberation/classification and a lower-complexity Ag-bearing concentrate route
Data extraction status: Publisher abstract and highlights; full tables not independently extracted
Verification status: DOI, authors, journal metadata and abstract values checked on publisher page
Value provenance: 70% and 80% are author-reported Ag partition results
Interpretation and data handling notes: Do not average EVAc and MP results or treat either as a universal silver recovery range.

Authors: James Malumbo Mwase; Stefanie Wahl; Sylke Meyer; Duygu Yilmaz
Peer-review status: MDPI journal article; published after peer review
Research question: Can sequential leaching recover Ag and Al from a PV silicon-cell fraction while managing Pb?
Feed material: Manufactured and supplied silicon solar cells from the IFE Soltek department

Module or cell technology: Silicon solar cells; commercial cell type not specified in the extracted section
Initial feed mass, if reported: 20 g per leaching test; 200 mL solution stated for test work
Initial silver concentration: Untreated milled-cell assay 19,496 ppm Ag, or 1.9496 wt%, reported in Table 3
Concentration basis: Milled cell fraction, not whole module
Separation method: Sequential laboratory leaching, precipitation and product reduction; hazardous wet chemistry conducted by the study in a fume hood
Experimental conditions: Paper reports HCl pre-leach and HNO3 Ag leach. The study's detailed hazardous procedure is not reproduced here.
Silver recovery, if measured: 99% Ag extraction in the second leach; overall Ag recovery about 98% after precipitation, reported by authors
Silver concentration in product: Authors report metallic silver product above 99.9% purity by XRF, with possible Pb and Fe contamination
Other reported recovery metrics: Paper reports about 99% Al extraction; Pb removal from solution also reported
Analytical method: ICP-MS on digested feed/residue; XRF and XRD for process/product characterization
Number of replicates, if reported: Two best-result samples are emphasized; authors state tests were repeated but complete replication counts are not captured
Measurement uncertainty: Not stated for the headline Ag recovery in the accessible paper
Energy or reagent consumption: Multiple acid/base/reduction reagents, heated leaching and waste-stream treatment; lifecycle totals not reported
Main findings: High author-reported Ag extraction and product purity from a prepared cell feed, with associated reagent and effluent-management burden
Study limitations: Laboratory-scale chemicals and cell feed are not whole-module processing; several proposed flowsheet steps remain conceptual; exact mass-weighted Ag closure not independently recalculated here

Data extraction status: Full open-access paper reviewed, including methods, Table 1, Table 3 and conclusions
Verification status: DOI, metadata, material basis, assay and reported extraction figures verified from article PDF
Numerical value source location: Pages 2-3 methods and Table 1; page 6 Table 3; pages 6-8 conclusions
Value provenance: 19,496 ppm and residue assays author-reported ICP-MS values; extraction/purity values are author-reported
Interpretation and data handling notes: Concentration changes alone do not replace a mass-weighted Ag balance. Do not present the chemistry as an AGASTYA procedure.

Full paper title: Effect of Temperature on the Glass Delamination in End-of-Life of Crystalline Silicon Photovoltaic Panels
Authors: Soroush Khakpour; Francesco Nocera; Alberta Latteri; Claudio Tosto; Lorena Saitta
Research question: How does thermal softening temperature change glass delamination and residue morphology?
Feed material: Laminated glass-EVA-cell specimens from a decommissioned module
Feed preparation: Frame and junction box removed; laminate cut to 15 by 15 cm coupons
Module or cell technology: 370 Wp monocrystalline module, ECO-370M-60EHC, about 25 years in service
Concentration basis: Thermal coupon delamination, not silver recovery
Separation method: Oven-assisted EVA softening followed by manual glass peel
Experimental conditions: 100 C or 140 C for 60 minutes; peel about 45 degrees and 20-30 N
Other reported recovery metrics: Six independent coupons per temperature condition; residue morphology differs by condition
Analytical method: TGA, DSC, FTIR, SEM and digital force gauge
Measurement uncertainty: No uncertainty values for Ag or process yield; coupon count and qualitative consistency reported
Energy or reagent consumption: 60-minute oven treatment; numerical energy consumption not reported
Main findings: Temperature affected failure mode and residue; 140 C gave smoother separation but thicker residue, while 100 C gave more fragmented residue
Study limitations: Single module family and oven/manual peel method; not a hot-knife validation or universal operating setpoint
Relevance to AGASTYA: Evidence for optional Stage 1/2 thermal pretreatment and a possible coupon study design, not an Ag recovery result
Verification status: DOI, paper metadata, methods, coupon count and reported conditions checked
Numerical value source location: Publisher Abstract, Materials and Methods, and Conclusions
Value provenance: Coupon conditions and n are author-reported experimental settings
Interpretation and data handling notes: Do not reuse 100 C or 140 C as AGASTYA settings without a measured material and supervised validation.

Research question: Can a full-size PV module cohesive-zone model explain preferential delamination locations under thermal and aging conditions?
Feed material: Model of commercial c-Si module, not an AGASTYA sample
Feed preparation: Abaqus cohesive-zone finite-element model; thermal cycles and aging conditions

Concentration basis: No silver calculation; structural delamination model
Separation method: Cohesive-zone interface model under thermal cycling

Relevance to AGASTYA: Thermal delamination simulation is plausible only after matched material/interface data and validation exist
Data extraction status: Publisher abstract and indexed article text reviewed
Verification status: DOI, author list, date, journal metadata, model class and limitations checked on publisher page
Numerical value source location: Publisher Abstract, Numerical Model and Conclusion snippets
Value provenance: Model findings reported by authors; no new AGASTYA solver output
Interpretation and data handling notes: The prior five-node thermal resistance model is not equivalent to this validated CZM model.
